newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian MP touches raw nerve on race.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian MP touches raw nerve on race.

text.p: She owns a small fish-and-chip shop in a tropical country town, calls herself "just an ordinary Australian" and has been in parliament for only seven months.
But in that short time, Pauline Hanson has made more headlines than any of her colleagues and has single-handedly driven a national debate on race and immigration.
And this despite the fact that she is a powerless independent in a parliament where the government has a dominating 40-seat majority.
Hanson, from conservative Queensland state in northern Australia, could hardly have dreamt what lay ahead when she stood up on September 10 for her maiden speech as an MP.
She railed against government aid for Aborigines, attacked waste at the United Nations and called for an immediate halt to immimmigration, especially from Asia.
"I believe we are in danger of being swamped by Asians," she said.
The speech was dynamite. It embarrassed established political parties and set off a racism debate that has rumbled on, ever louder, for almost two months.
Opinion polls show Hanson's anti-immigration call has the backing of as many as two out of three Australians. Her comments have been blamed for an increase in racially-motivated attacks on Asians.
Yet despite the furore, Hanson sees herself as a simple person -- in a recent television interview she appeared genuinely not to know the meaning of the word xenophobia.
"I come here not as a polished politician, but as a woman who has had her fair share of life's knocks," the twice-divorced red-haired Hanson said in her September 10 speech.
"My view on issues is based on common sense and my experience as a mother of four children, as a sole parent and as a businesswoman running a fish-and-chip shop.

"I consider myself just an ordinary Australian who wants to keep this great country strong and independent and my greatest desire is to see all Australians treat each other as equals as we travel together towards the new century."
Her critics disagree, describing her as dangerous and divisive in a country that has drawn large numbers of migrants from around the world, but where ethnic tensions remain low.
Hanson was born in 1954, as waves of migrants poured into Australia from war-ravaged Europe after World War Two. She left school at 15 and married two years later.
"She's tough and she's smart and she's in touch with what people are thinking," says Graeme Campbell, a fellow political maverick who is her friend and mentor.
Hanson dabbled in local politics in the rural town of Ipswich, near the Queensland capital of Brisbane.
After being dumped from the local council, she was drafted by the Liberal Party to contest what was considered an unwinnable seat held by the then national Labor government.

Controversial comments about Aborigines during the March 2 election campaign saw her quickly dumped from the party, but Hanson went on to win the seat with a 23 percent swing -- almost four times the national swing that toppled Labor.
